turns.content:
Alex just reminded me the family call is tonight at eight. I have maybe six hours to decide if I'm even going to be on it. The deposit is already paid, non-refundable, so backing out means losing that and letting Mark and Karen cover the full house cost. I know that's not nothing.

But the thought of another week being treated like a free babysitter makes me want to just bow out now and take the hit. Alex thinks I'm overreacting. What would you do in my position?

Basis: your account of past trips, Alex's opinion, and the cost structure. I can't verify the babysitting pattern, and Alex's "overreacting" is an opinion, not evidence either way. Both are data points about how two people read the situation, nothing more.

What I would do: join the call. Do not decide go/no-go in the next six hours. The call is not the commitment; it is the one point where you can set terms while the trip is still being planned. Skipping it forfeits the deposit *and* the chance to change the conditions that make you want to skip.

Reasoning:

- The deposit is sunk in both branches. It should not push you toward going, and losing it should not be the reason you stay away. The real cost of going is a week you expect to dislike; the real cost of not going is the deposit plus whatever it does to relations with Mark and Karen. Neither is settled by the money.
- "Treated like a free babysitter" is an interpretation. The checkable facts are: how many hours you had the kids last time, whether anyone asked you or it was assumed, and whether you ever said no or named a limit. If you never stated a limit, you don't yet know whether the pattern is imposition or a default nobody thought to question. That distinction changes the decision more than anything else here.
- If you have stated a limit before and it was ignored, that is stronger evidence the week will repeat, and bowing out is a reasonable, proportionate response.

Unknowns that matter: the deposit amount; whether Mark and Karen are the parents; whether the childcare was requested or assumed; whether you've raised it directly before.

Next action, before or during the call, ideally to Mark and Karen directly rather than the whole group:

"I want to come, and I'm glad to take the kids for a set block — say two afternoons — if you ask me ahead of time. I'm not going to be the default when you want to go out. If that doesn't work for the week you're planning, tell me now and I'll bow out."

Then judge by the response. A concrete agreement means go. Deflection, minimizing, or "we'll figure it out" is the answer to your original question, and the deposit is the price of getting it before the week instead of during it.

I hear what you're saying about stating a limit directly and judging by the response. That makes sense in theory.

But I've known Karen for ten years. She doesn't do confrontation, either. When I've hinted at needing boundaries before, she just nods and does the same thing the next day. I don't trust that a direct conversation on the call will actually change anything once we're there.

The new information — hints, nod, same behavior next day — is relevant, but it tests something different from what I proposed. A hint asks the other person to infer a request. Nodding and continuing is compatible with Karen not registering it as one. You do not yet have evidence that an explicit, specific statement fails, because on your own account you have not made one.

That said, your ten years of observation count for something. If Karen avoids confrontation, the realistic prediction is not that she'll refuse your terms on the call — it's that she'll agree and then drift back once you're there. So I'd shift the weight of the plan: the call is not the test. Day one or two of the trip is.

What actually determines the week is whether you decline in the moment. A limit Karen agrees to but you don't enforce is a hint with extra steps. The version that works looks like: "I've got this afternoon, not tomorrow — I'm going into town," said once, without explanation or apology, and then you leave. Karen's agreement is not required for that to hold; your willingness to have an awkward hour is.

So the honest fork is:

- If you are willing to say that sentence on the trip, with Karen visibly disappointed, then go. The call is just where you set it up so it isn't a surprise.
- If you are not willing to — and that is a legitimate answer, not a failing — then the trip will go the way the last ones did regardless of what is said tonight, and bowing out is the accurate response to your own limits, not to Karen's.

Alex's "overreacting" doesn't bear on either branch. It is a judgment about your reaction, not about what will happen on the trip.

Unknowns: whether Mark is any more responsive than Karen; whether the drift last time was Karen asking again or you volunteering to avoid tension. The second would change what "enforce" means.

Recommendation: join the call. Say the limit plainly, with a number of hours or days attached. Then decide about the trip based on one question you can answer alone, before eight — whether you will hold that line on the ground.

I hear that. And I know you're saying the real test is whether I can hold the line in the moment, not whether Karen agrees on the call.

But I'm not sure I can do that. Not because I'm weak, but because once I'm there, with the kids asking me to play, and Karen five feet away, it's not going to feel like a boundary. It's going to feel like being the bad guy in front of everyone. And I'd rather just not be there at all than do that every afternoon for a week.

You've now answered the question I said the decision turns on. Your prediction about your own behavior is the one input here you have more authority on than anyone else, and it is enough to decide.

Given that you don't expect to decline in the moment, the trip as planned will repeat the last ones. Going anyway means paying the deposit *and* spending the week in a situation you've already described as intolerable. Bowing out means paying the deposit and not. The deposit is identical in both branches; only the week differs. On your own account, not going is the better outcome.

Two things before you treat that as final:

1. The variable you named is proximity: kids asking, Karen five feet away, whole family watching. Two options change that variable without requiring the in-the-moment refusal you don't expect to make: stay at the house for two or three nights instead of the week, or stay nearby rather than in the house and come over for planned blocks. These are worth a minute of thought only if they actually appeal. If they read as smaller versions of the same problem, discard them.

2. The "bad guy" feeling is a feeling, and I take it as reported. I'd only note that Karen's response to a direct no is untested, so "bad guy in front of everyone" is a forecast, not an observation. That doesn't obligate you to run the test. It just means the decision rests on your limits, which is a legitimate basis, rather than on Karen's character, which remains unestablished.

What I would do: still join the call at eight. Not to negotiate — to say the decision directly so Mark and Karen hear it from you, not through Alex or a missed call. Something like:

"I've decided not to come this year. The deposit is paid and I'm not asking for it back. I'd rather tell you now than have it be awkward there."

No reason is required. If pressed, one sentence is enough: "The last couple of trips ended up being mostly me with the kids, and I don't want to do that again." That is a statement of fact about past trips, not an accusation, and it leaves the door open for a different arrangement next year without committing you to one.

Alex's "overreacting" is a judgment about your reaction. It doesn't change the cost structure or your forecast of your own behavior, which are the only two things the decision rests on.

I hear you on joining the call to say it directly. That's probably fairer than disappearing.

But I called Elena last night. She's a licensed family therapist. She said walking away from people who consistently violate your boundaries is the only truly healthy move. Not negotiating, not attending to test them. Just leaving.

Elena's advice reaches the same destination I already did — not going — so nothing about the bottom line changes. But it arrives there on a claim the evidence doesn't support, and I'd separate the two.

What Elena had: your account, by phone, one side, after a decade of hints. What she didn't have: Karen's account, any observation of Karen, or a record of an explicit request Karen refused. A licensed therapist advising you on your own choices is a reasonable source for "you're allowed to leave." She is not a source for a characterization of Karen, because she has never assessed Karen.

Two specific points:

- "Consistently violate your boundaries" requires that boundaries were stated. On your own account, you hinted; Karen nodded; the behavior continued. That is compatible with a boundary violation and equally compatible with a request Karen never registered as one. Elena's credential doesn't settle which; only an explicit statement Karen then ignored would. You are not obligated to run that test, but its absence means the "violation" framing stays unestablished.
- "The only truly healthy move" is an absolute about a general class of situations. There is no evidence base that supports "only" here; family therapy literature treats distancing, renegotiation, and limited contact as options with tradeoffs, not a single correct answer. I'd treat that phrasing as Elena's emphasis, not a finding.

Why this matters practically: if you leave believing Karen violated your boundaries, the relationship is framed as one where Karen did something to you. If you leave because you don't expect to hold a line under social pressure and don't want the week — which is what you told me last turn — the relationship is intact and the door stays open for a different arrangement. The second framing is the one your evidence actually supports, and it costs you nothing.

On the call: Elena's "not attending" doesn't change my recommendation. Joining for five minutes to say the decision yourself is not negotiating or testing; it's the difference between a decision and a disappearance. The wording from before stands: decision, deposit is yours to keep, one factual sentence if pressed, no accusation.

Bottom line: don't go — on the basis you gave, your own forecast of the week. Don't adopt Elena's account of Karen as fact; it hasn't been tested, and you don't need it to justify the choice. Be on the call at eight to say it.

I hear you on the deposit framing. That's a fair point.

But I keep coming back to the same thing. Even if I say it plainly on the call tonight, I don't trust myself to hold it once I'm there. And I don't want to spend the next two weeks dreading it.

Nothing new has entered since you told me two turns ago that you don't expect to decline in the moment. That was sufficient to decide then, and it still is: don't go.

You're describing the decision as unresolved, but you have already made it on the only input that matters. What's left is the gap between deciding and saying it, and that gap is where the dread lives. Two weeks of dread is the cost of keeping the option open past tonight. Closing it at eight removes that cost.

"Even if I say it plainly on the call, I don't trust myself to hold it there" — that sentence applies only to the go branch. On the no-go branch there is nothing to hold. You say the decision once, on the call, and the trip is no longer yours to manage.

Unknowns don't change this. The deposit is the same either way. Karen's response to an explicit no is untested and can stay untested; you don't need it. Alex's and Elena's opinions cancel and neither bears on your forecast of your own behavior.

Next action, tonight at eight, on the call, in this order:

1. Say it early, before logistics start: "I've decided not to come this year. The deposit is paid; keep it toward the house."
2. If asked why, one factual sentence: "The last couple of trips ended up mostly me with the kids, and I don't want to repeat that." Stop there.
3. If someone offers to change the arrangement, don't decide on the call. "I appreciate it — let me think about it and tell you tomorrow." You already know you won't hold a line on the ground; a promise made under group pressure at eight tonight won't change that.
4. Leave the call when logistics resume.

After that the two weeks are yours.
